title: PCIe Topology Fragmentation and Runtime Fallback Mitigation
author: Asha Patel
content:
Summary:

This page documents a class of production incidents we have observed where PCIe / host topology fragmentation (uneven NUMA/PCIe root complex attachments and NVLink islands) produces unpredictable kernel scheduling outcomes, degraded throughput, or cascaded fallbacks to lower-fidelity execution paths. The doc explains symptoms, root causes, automated detection heuristics, immediate mitigations, and medium-term fixes plus an incident runbook for oncall.

Why this matters:
- Manifestation: single-tenant or multi-tenant kernels exhibit large variance in tail latency and per-token GPU time (20–400% increases) under certain placement patterns.
- Impacted features: large autoregressive generation, streaming responses, batching-heavy endpoints, multi-model pipelines with chained KV cache usage.
- Business impact: SLA violations on 99th percentile latency, elevated per-token costs, and repeated model fallback/eviction cycles that reduce quality for users.

Scope and applicability:
- Affects clusters with mixed PCIe/NVLink topologies (common in our Dedicated and Private deployments when mixes of A100, H100, and earlier generation cards are used).
- Observed when node-level device allocation policies route co-resident critical kernels to devices across distinct PCIe root complexes or across an NVLink boundary.

Symptoms (observable signals):
1) Stepwise increase in kernel wall-time correlated with specific placement decisions (per-kernel wall-time jump of 3–10x).
2) Elevated scheduler preemption and reroute events (trace tags: scheduler.reassign, kernel.handoff).
3) Rapid increase in fallback-to-lower-fidelity model variants or disabled tensor-core paths.
4) Device-to-device throughput variance visible in node telemetry (NVLink bandwidth metrics asymmetry).

Quick triage checklist (oncall):
1) Identify affected pod/workload: check request trace and model variant.
   - Commands:
     - kubectl -n redwood get pods -o wide | grep <instance-id>
     - rg "request-id=<id>" /var/log/serving/requests.log
2) Correlate with node device topology: run on suspected host:
   - lspci | rg -A1 -i nvidia
   - sudo nvidia-smi topo -m
   - | Example output: "GPU0 GPU1 CPU0 CPU1
     GPU0 X NVLINK SYS SYS
     GPU1 NVLINK X SYS SYS"
3) Inspect runtime kernel traces and scheduler events (trace tags):
   - curl http://localhost:8100/debug/trace?request=<id> | jq .events | rg topology
4) Check for recent placement changes or cluster autoscaler events in the same timespan.

Root cause patterns (typical):
- Placement across PCIe root complexes: co-scheduled sub-tasks of a single request land on GPUs with expensive host hops.
- NVLink island mismatch: pinned KV cache or attention cache spans GPUs without high-bandwidth interconnect, forcing expensive host-mediated transfers.
- Fragmented allocator state: per-device memory fragmentation makes the scheduler attempt split allocations that require cross-device coordination.
- Healed device affinity fallthrough: the admission controller moves work to an available GPU that is topologically distant to reduce queueing, which worsens latency.

Table: symptom => short-term mitigation => medium-term fix
| Symptom | Short-term mitigation | Medium-term fix |
|---|---|---|
| Kernel wall-time spike when GPU hops cross NVLink | Evict non-critical background cohorts from affected host; enable same-node placement policy for the request | Topology-aware allocator and routing policy (see design below) |
| KV cache misses due to remote device eviction | Increase ephemeral routing priority for cached session tokens or pin cache to single NVLink island | Cache-aware placement + capacity reservation for cache-heavy cohorts |
| Scheduler reassign thrash | Raise preemption threshold and enable backoff window 30s | Admission-control refinement: topology penalty scoring + binding reservations |

Immediate mitigations (playbook actions):
- Emergency stabilization (2–5 minutes):
  1) Put the affected node(s) into cordon state to prevent new allocations: kubectl cordon <node>.
  2) Identify and migrate non-critical low-priority cohorts off the node (evict pods with priorityClassName: low).
  3) If the node hosts canary or experimental kernels, roll them back to the previous runtime version (release tag).
- Short window guard (10–30 minutes):
  1) Flip the scheduler flag runtime.scheduler.topology_penalty_multiplier=2.0 (temporary) via config-svc: curl -X PATCH $CONFIG_SVC/api/v1/flags -d '{"topology_penalty_multiplier":2.0}'.
  2) Enable topology-aware binding for the service route: patch route config to bindingMode: strict-local for critical endpoints.
  3) Monitor 99p latency, kernel wall-time, and NVLink drop counters.

Runbook: step-by-step incident handling
1) Detect
   - Alert trigger: 99th-percentile generation latency > SLO * 1.5 for 5 minutes AND scheduler.reassign events > 50/min across a host cluster.
2) Contain
   - Action: Cordon and drain non-critical pods; set node annotation redwood/isolated=true to prevent autoscaler reattachment.
3) Diagnose
   - Collect: nvidia-smi topo -m, dmesg | tail -n 200, runtime trace for request IDs, allocator map: curl $RUNTIME/api/v1/allocator/slots?node=<node>&json=true
   - Note: allocator map endpoint returns a large JSON; save to /tmp/alloc-<node>-YYYYMMDD.json for postmortem.
4) Mitigate
   - If KV-cache eviction found: restore pinned cache by restarting cache-manager with parameter --pin-to-island=GPU0,GPU1.
   - If scheduler is reassigning across root complexes: set runtime.scheduler.force_coalition_binding=true for the affected cohort.
5) Restore
   - Uncordon hosts once stable for 10 minutes; revert temporary flags after rolling config change to final topology-aware policy.
6) Postmortem
   - Assign engineer to root cause investigation and timeline; attach traces and config diffs; classify severity and action items.

Debugging artifacts to collect (commands):
- sudo nvidia-smi topo -m > /tmp/topo-<node>.txt
- sudo lspci -vvv | rg -A3 -i nvidia > /tmp/lspci-<node>.txt
- curl $RUNTIME/debug/trace?node=<node>&range=10m > /tmp/trace-<node>.json
- cat /var/log/syslog | rg -i "nvlink|pci|nvidia|oom" > /tmp/syslog-device.txt

Medium-term design proposal (owner: runtime kernel team):
1) Topology-aware scheduler scoring: augment the current scheduler score with a topology penalty term computed from an undirected graph of device connectivity. Score = base_score - alpha * locality_bonus + beta * topology_penalty.
2) KV-cache affinity reservations: allow session tokens to create light-weight reservations within an NVLink island. Reservation semantics: soft_hold (30s) and hard_hold (configurable per-cohort).
3) Allocator compaction and defragmentation daemon: periodic compaction job per node that coalesces free blocks and emits health metrics.
4) Admission controller policy: route requests through a topology advisory function that returns a placement recommendation; fallback to cost-based placement only if advisory cannot satisfy SLO.

Configuration examples:
- Scheduler flag patch (example curl):
  curl -X PATCH https://config.redwood-internal/v1/flags
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json'
    -d '{"runtime.scheduler.topology_penalty_multiplier":"1.5"}'

- Example admission policy snippet (YAML):
  apiVersion: redwood/v1
  kind: RouteBindingPolicy
  metadata:
    name: cache-heavy-binding
  spec:
    bindingMode: "prefer-local-island"
    topologyHints:
      nvlink_weight: 10
      pcie_weight: 5
    reservations:
      soft_hold_seconds: 30
      hard_hold_seconds: 300

Metrics and dashboards to monitor (suggested panels):
- Kernel wall-time by placement type (local-island vs cross-root): 99/95/50 percentiles.
- NVLink utilization and per-link asymmetry heatmap.
- Scheduler reassign / handoff rate per host.
- KV-cache miss ratio per session cohort.
- Incident guard: nodes with recent topology_penalty overrides.

Testing and benchmark guidance:
- Synthetic reproduction: use our workload-synth harness with --placement-pattern topology_cross and --burst-shape {microburst, sustained}. Benchmark matrix should include: sequence lengths 64, 512, 2048; batch sizes 1, 8, 32; and model variants with and without KV cache.
- Kernel-level microbench: run schedule_with_topology_probe binary on target host; collect microtraces and compare median kernel launch latencies across islands.

Rollout plan for topology-aware scheduler (phased):
1) Canary (QA): small internal cluster with mixed topologies; run 48-hour soak with workload-synth corpora.
2) Beta (limited customer): enable on Dedicated regions with annotation-based opt-in.
3) Gradual ramp: 10% -> 50% -> 100% traffic over 2–4 weeks with rollback gates on 99p latency and per-token cost.

Ownership and escalation path:
- Primary owner: eng-serving-runtime/kernel-scheduling (rotation: @kernel-oncall).
- Secondary: eng-infra/gpu-fleet (pager: @gpu-oncall).
- Escalation to SRE and Product if SLA risk > 4 hours.

Related pages:
- runtime-architecture/execution-stitching-and-fallback-orchestration-2026
- kernel-and-scheduling/scheduler-telemetry-synthesis-and-proofing-2025

Post-incident action items (examples):
- Add topology-awareness unit tests to scheduler CI (owner: kernel team).
- Instrument allocator to surface fragmentation percentiles per-device.
- Document preferred hardware mixes for Dedicated offers (product + infra).

Appendix: diagnostic outputs (example snippets)
- Example nvidia-smi topo -m excerpt:
  "GPU0   GPU1   CPU0   CPU1
   GPU0    X    NVLINK SYS   SYS
   GPU1  NVLINK    X   SYS   SYS"
- Example trace event line: trace_event{timestamp:162..., tag:"kernel.handoff", payload:"from=GPU0,to=GPU3,reason=affinity_fallback,delta_ms=245"}

Notes and rationale:
- We prefer conservative short-term mitigations that prioritize availability and predictable latency over immediate throughput gains. The topology-aware scheduler balances quality with economics by default but can be tuned per-customer.
